"Kill Hijikata Toshizō."
That such a thing came to be seriously debated within Itō's faction dates from about this time.

Around this time — that is to say, just when the talk of the Shinsengumi being lifted out of its standing as rōnin held in the charge of the Kyoto Protector, and taken up into the direct service of the Tokugawa house, was beginning to take concrete shape.
In terms of the Shinsengumi's own chronicle, it was about the time they met their fourth autumn in the capital.
Early autumn, the second year of Keiō.
The staff officer Itō Kashitarō, for the record,
"was holding a memorial service for old comrades from the Edo days"—
such was the notice he filed with the corps; and he gathered the leading men of his faction at Kaikō-ji, a sub-temple within the grounds of Sennyū-ji in the eastern hills of Kyoto.

Those who gathered: besides such weighty figures as Itō's own younger brother Suzuki Mikisaburō, captain of the Shinsengumi's Ninth Unit, and the inspector Shinohara Tainoshin, there were Utsumi Jirō and Nakanishi Noboru, live-in pupils of Itō's swordsmanship; and the corporal Kanō Michinosuke, Hattori Takeo, and the inspector Arai Tadao, comrades of Itō's since the Edo days.
Besides these, just one man, was mixed in from outside the Shinsengumi.
This man sat silent, in an attitude as if he were embracing a pillar.
A room in the abbot's quarters of Kaikō-ji was the meeting-place; beyond the veranda lay a garden thick with shrubs, taking in the cliff of the Eastern Hills.
Early autumn it was, yet the sunlight was hot.
The wind came falling down from about the old, great maple at the top of the cliff.
"Itō-san, break away. That's the one move. There's no call now for hard talk or scheming, is there?"

said Shinohara Tainoshin. After the Restoration this rōnin from Kurume took the name Hata Shigechika and entered official service, soon retired to his ease, and died at the ripe age of eighty-four in the last years of Meiji; there was something easygoing about him, and he disliked troublesome intrigue.
"You, now, Itō-san,"
said Shinohara. A comrade of Itō's since the Edo days, he was seven or eight years the elder.
"you can't let go. Even with matters come to this, you still mean to seize the Shinsengumi and make it a loyalist army for the Emperor, don't you."
"I do."

"A man of many schemes. True enough, the Shinsengumi as it stands has turned over three times. First Kiyokawa Hachirō made it; next Serizawa Kamo was struck down and Kondō's faction took it over. The fourth turn would be Itō Kashitarō."
said Shinohara, tapping the nape of his neck with his iron war-fan,
"but will the wholesaler sell it that cheap? The Shinsengumi as it is has a cooper on the premises."
"A cooper?"

"Hijikata, I mean. Back in Bushū the fellow peddled medicine, they say, but a cooper is what he really is. He planes the staves flush and draws the hoops so tight that you could pitch a boulder in and they'd not spring loose."
"Shinohara-kun, you see him well."
Itō Kashitarō smiled.
"That cooper—"
"shall we cut him down?"
"Just so."
Itō nodded, and went on,

"Once Hijikata is dead, all that's left is that fool Kondō. Talk him round and he comes over to the Emperor's side. I've been with him more than once on the road through the Chūgoku country, and I'm sure of it. The poor man has a weakness — he loves the sound of politics, of ideas. I'll bring him round, see if I don't."
"So the problem is the cooper."
Shinohara said, chuckling,
"but he's strong."
Smack — he struck the base of his neck with the iron fan. An autumn fly dropped, rolling, onto his knee.
"Shinohara-kun, I have not asked that you be the one to do it."
said Itō.
"Will you do it with numbers?"
"Well — that is what I mean to discuss."
"If you cut him down, it must be one man alone."
said Shinohara, and picking up the fly he rose and went to the veranda, and there flung it away.

"Itō-san, unless one man does it, this business will come out. Let it be found out, and there's trouble. Kondō's a fool, so he'll fly into a rage and take his revenge; and any drawing him over to the Emperor's cause will come to nothing."
"That, too, is in my thoughts."
and Itō glanced toward the pillar of the veranda.
There the man in question sat.
He was smoking tobacco. His fox-brown skin, one half of the face catching the glare off the garden, showed a faint blue, as though a thin moss had grown over it.
The lips were thin, and from the right side of the nose a single crease ran down to the corner of the mouth.
Six years.
This man, too, had aged.
It was Shichiri Kennosuke, once the head pupil of the Kōgen Ittō-ryū dōjō at Hachiōji in Bushū.

He had drifted from lodging to lodging in the Chōshū and Satsuma mansions, but by now he was one of the leading men among the loyalist rōnin of Kyoto. It was Shichiri's doing, too, that Itō Kashitarō had been brought to Nakamura Hanjirō of Satsuma — the man later known as Kirino Toshiaki.
"The truth is, Shichiri-san here"
said Itō,

"tells me he wishes to gather a band of rōnin and cut the man down. As Shichiri-san sees it, if we do it ourselves it is certain to leak out. He offers to act in our stead. For us it is a poor showing, and I blush at it, but if he will do it so, the work after comes the easier — the drawing of Kondō to us, and the making of the corps into a loyalist army."
"But, Shichiri-san — how are you to lure out that wary cooper?"
said Shinohara, turning his face toward the veranda.
In the backlight sat Shichiri Kennosuke. Tap — he knocked the bowl of his pipe against the ash-pot, and spoke in a very small voice.
"I know that man's nature. Ours is an old acquaintance, after all."
"It would seem there is some grudge in it."

"No — it is for the Imperial land. To make the Shinsengumi into an army for the overthrow of the shogunate, a risk of this order is nothing at all. Strike down that one cooper you speak of, and the hoops of the Shinsengumi spring apart, every one."
The next day, Itō Kashitarō, taking his confidant Arai Tadao, set out for Nagoya in Owari.
—The movements of the Owari Tokugawa house are delicate.

said Itō; to go and observe that situation was the reason he gave Kondō, but his true aim was an exchange of views with the loyalist party within the Owari domain. Or rather, behind that lay one further, truer motive.
While he was away, Shichiri would kill Hijikata Toshizō. The corps would no doubt be thrown into an uproar, and this was his precaution against being caught up in it.
—Shichiri-san, I shall be back in the capital after the twentieth of the ninth month. I should like the work done by then.
he had impressed on him.
Toshizō—
knew nothing of it, of course.
Glad that Kondō had of late settled into the barracks, he left the corps' inner affairs to him and went out often on patrol through the city.
He always took one unit or another with him, turn by turn.
When Toshizō went out into the streets of Kyoto, it was said, the broad ways and the narrow alike fell silent, as still as if water had been sprinkled to lay the dust.
That day, taking Okita Sōji's unit, he left the barracks toward dusk.

He watched the sun set before the Sannō shrine at Takatsuji. Looking back, beyond the great ginkgo in the precincts, the sun was going down, letting its red light drip onto the clouds of the western hills.
"Master Hōgyoku, will no verse come to you?"
teased Okita.
"Autumn verse doesn't come easy for me."
"Of the four seasons, then, which season-word suits you?"
"Spring."
"Hmm."
Okita made a face, as if to say, there's a surprising thing.
"Hijikata-san — spring, is it?"
"Have you some objection?"
"No objection in particular, but—"
"Spring's my season."
And indeed, in that "Hōgyoku Hokku Album" that Okita had once peeked into, the spring verses were overwhelmingly the most numerous.
At a glance one would have thought that a man of his nature would favor the bone-chilling season-feel of winter.
"They say a man who loves the spring is one who always sets his hopes on the morrow."
"Is that so."
They went north up the Higashi-no-tōin.
From here as far as the Rokkaku, the Kyoto mansions of the various domains stand thick: Minakuchi, Geishū Hiroshima, Satsuma, Oshi, Iyo Matsuyama.
Even the domain samurai posted to Kyoto hereabouts, meeting a Shinsengumi patrol in the road, would quietly give way.
When they came to the corner of the Takoyakushi, the men all lit their lanterns.
"Sōji, I've a little errand in mind. I'll stroll on a way alone, so let's part here."
"Where will you be going?"
Okita did not ask.
Okita had a dim notion of where Toshizō was bound.
"Take care, then."
"Aye."
Toshizō walked west along the Takoyakushi.
It was the house of the woman in question. Oyuki.
The woman was there. As though she had been waiting for Toshizō to come, she was lightly made up.
"I happened to be nearby—"
said Toshizō, turning his eyes away from the woman's face. For this man to show even so much shyness was a thing unheard of.
"Am I a nuisance?"
"No. Please come up. I'll make tea directly."
This was the seventh or eighth time he had called, and Oyuki's manner had grown quite soft.
Yet Toshizō did not so much as take Oyuki's hand. Somehow — and it was unlike the man — with Oyuki alone he had no wish to behave so.
Always he made small talk and went home.
Talk of Edo. Of his childhood. Of gidayū chanting. Of the doings of the Kyoto streets.
Before Oyuki, Toshizō became a very talkative man. Had Kondō or Okita watched him from some hidden place, they would have thought him another person.
Of his childhood, above all, he talked as though there were no end to it.
Oyuki was a clever listener. She nodded at each turn, gave a low, well-pitched laugh, and now and then, demurely, threw his own words back at him.
Toshizō spoke with a strange ardor. When it came to memories especially, he grew heated.
It was an ardor as if he wished to leave the whole of his one life told and handed down to Oyuki.
"My mother, now. She died when I was three."
It was talk that, to another's ear, would have seemed too foolish for words.
"Oyuki-san. Do you know the place in Bushū they call Takahata Fudō?"
"Yes — the name only."
"My mother came from that village. For a woman, they say, she was fond of drink. My elder sister Onobu took that blood too — of a night she never fails to empty a flask or two."
"And this Onobu-sama stood in your mother's place, then."

"That was her intention, I suppose. But I took more to my sister's husband, Satō Hikogorō, than to my sister, and I was more often at the Satō house in Hino-juku than at my birth-home in Ishida village. The man was headman of the whole Hino district, and since my father's time a patron of our Tennen Rishin-ryū. My brother-in-law Hikogorō is a licensed hand with the sword, too."
"And your elder sister Onobu—"
Oyuki's interest ran rather to the sister,
"she took after your mother, I suppose?"
"In the drink alone. In face and temper, they say, not at all. My mother — I was too young, of course, to remember her — but by what my sister and brothers tell me, at her drink she was like—"
and, having begun, Toshizō shut his mouth.
How was it he had never noticed until now, he wondered; a small discovery had come to him. It burst with a snap within his breast and spread, filling it, into astonishment.
(She is like this woman.)
At last he understood, himself, why he came so often and so intently to this house.

The woman Oyuki fit none of the molds of the women he had until now taken up as suited to his taste. If anything, she was of a type that the old Toshizō, with his fondness for high birth, ought to have found of no interest whatever. Yet he was drawn to her. The reason he could not, himself, well understand.
"What is it?"
"It's nothing…"
Toshizō softly took up from beside his knee the thin Kyoto-ware sencha cup,
and, as if idly, changed the subject.
"I wanted to be a samurai, you see."
"Eh?"

"I mean, I did. So as a boy I planted arrow-bamboo in the garden of my birth-home. I'd heard that a warrior's house in the Warring States days always planted arrow-bamboo, and so I said I would do the same, and planted it."
His talk had no stopping-place.
And to Toshizō's aimless chatter Oyuki gave her assent, at each turn, as to something precious.
(This man does not come here to talk.)
Oyuki thought.
(He comes here to become, somehow, another self.)
It was not that he came to speak; rather, it seemed, Toshizō came to sound some other string within his own heart.
And yet, on the other hand,
(Oyuki is good.)
he thought, so much that it turned to sorrow.
(Someday I will hold her.)
Yet, thinking so, once he had come to this house he would spend what little time was his own on that same rambling chatter.
That night, it was past the hour of the Dog when he left Oyuki's house.
As he trod on the gutter-boards, the insects' cry ceased.
Stars filled the whole sky.
Toshizō went down the Aburanokōji and came out at a corner called Echigoya-chō.
Every house had its shutters down, but Toshizō knew that in this quarter one shop alone stood open — a shop called Yohei's, that sold saké and sweet saké.
He went in.
There was a customer before him.
Toshizō ordered sweet saké.
"Sweet saké, is it?"
The one who laughed was not old Yohei, the master. It was the customer who sat before him, in the dark of the corner. Laughing, he had loosened his blade in its scabbard.
Toshizō sat down on a bench a little apart.
"Shichiri, is it."
He was calm.

This dogged swordsman of the Kōgen Ittō-ryū had likely used some spy to trace even the fact that Toshizō went now and then to Oyuki's house. It may well be that this very night, from the moment Toshizō left Oyuki's house, one of Shichiri's spies had been on his trail.
Shichiri himself, no doubt, had gone on ahead into this shop of Yohei's and kept watch on the street.
"Sweet saké — how gentle of you."
and Shichiri rose from his own bench and came over to Toshizō's side.
"Are we to do it?"
said Toshizō.
"We are not."
Shichiri sat down facing Toshizō. Before him he set out, with a small clatter, his own flask, his cup, his dish of relishes, and—
"the two of us are bound too deep by fate; and yet it seems this is the first time we have come face to face like this, just the two of us,"
he said.
Toshizō held his silence.
"Hijikata, tonight let us talk at our leisure."
"I refuse."
and Toshizō raised his face. The sweet saké was brought.
"You won't talk? Deep as the bond may be, a bond of quarrels is no use to anyone, or so I reckon; but if you say you won't talk, then there's no help for it. A stubborn business."
"The stubborn one who keeps haunting me is you, I'd say. On the Horikawa I came near to losing my life."

"Hijikata, I don't know to which god your people made their vow when you were born, but you've had rare good fortune. Still, what do you say? This fated sort of bond doesn't suit my nature either, so shall the two of us try a rite for cutting the karma between us?"
"The two of us?"
"You too are a man they call Hijikata Toshizō. For a rite between man and man, to cut the karma, you'll not go calling for helpers or seconds."
"And you?"
"I am Shichiri Kennosuke. Old-fashioned as it is, I'll set it down for you on a Kumano oath-paper, if you like — though you, Hijikata, are not to be counted on."
"I am a samurai."
said Toshizō, shortly. A samurai. A grudge should be settled one man against one. —Shichiri Kennosuke, too, nodded, as though he had looked for Toshizō to answer just so, and said,
"I'll trust your word as a samurai. As for the time — set it for some later day and strange waters may seep in. Here and now — how would that be?"
"The place?"
Toshizō began, then at once pressed on:
"you'll leave that to me. It's the accepted rule that the one who takes up the challenge sets it."
He thought that if he let Shichiri name the spot there might be a trap in it.
"The Nijō riverbed — no one will come there."
"Good enough."
and with that Shichiri called at once toward the back of the shop.
"Master — will you call two kago for us?"
